title: Review an API that logs sensitive request data
description: Problem: Review an API that logs sensitive request data. Solve this problem with multiple approaches and detailed explanations.

data.text: An API logs the entire request body, headers, and query string to aid debugging. The logs contain passwords, credit card numbers, social security numbers, and authentication tokens. These logs are shipped to a central logging platform where engineers, support staff, and third-party log analyzers can read them. A single compromised log stream exposes every user's secrets, and the breach is rarely detected because log access is considered routine.

items: Understand what constitutes sensitive data under GDPR, CCPA, and PCI-DSS
Learn how structured logging frameworks capture request and response data by default
Identify common oversights: passwords in JSON bodies, auth tokens in headers, and PII in query strings
Apply data minimization: log events and metadata, not raw payloads

terms.definition: Personally identifiable information: any data that can identify a specific individual, such as name, email, or government ID.
Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard: a set of security requirements for handling credit card data.
Logging in a machine-readable format such as JSON, which makes it easy to query but also easy to accidentally include sensitive fields.
The principle of collecting and retaining only the data necessary for a specific purpose.

data.text: Logging sensitive data is a compliance violation and a security incident waiting to happen. Logs are stored for weeks or months, replicated across regions, and accessed by many people. A support engineer debugging a production issue can see a user's password in plain text. A log aggregation platform with a breach exposes thousands of credentials at once. Unlike a database breach, a log breach is rarely noticed because logs are not designed to be secret.

data.title: Logs are a data store
data.text: Anything you write to logs is persistent, searchable, and likely backed up. Treat logs with the same classification and access controls you apply to your primary database.

The problematic API uses a middleware or filter that serializes the entire HttpRequest into a log entry. It logs the body, headers, and query parameters without redaction. The developer added this for debugging and forgot to remove it. In production, every login, password change, and payment request writes secrets to the log stream.

data.title: Dangerous request logging middleware
data.content: A middleware that logs the full request without redaction:

data.text: The correct approach logs contextual metadata: the endpoint, user ID, request ID, duration, and status code. If you must log request data, redact sensitive fields before writing them. Use a centralized redaction library or middleware that knows which fields to mask. Never log authorization headers, cookies, or raw request bodies containing passwords or payment information.

data.title: Redacted request logging
data.content: Log request metadata and redact sensitive fields:

cards.title: Log everything
cards.description: Capture full request and response bodies for debugging.

cards.title: Log metadata only
cards.description: Log method, path, user ID, status, and duration.

cards.title: Log with redaction
cards.description: Log request data but replace sensitive values with masked tokens.
cons: Maintenance burden to update sensitive field list

cards.title: Conditional debug logging
cards.description: Log full details only when a debug flag is set for a specific user or request ID.
pros: No sensitive data in normal logs

data.title: Fields that must never appear in logs
items: Credit card numbers and CVV codes
Social security numbers and tax IDs
Authentication tokens, session IDs, and API keys
Medical record numbers and health information
Raw request bodies containing any of the above

data.title: Logs are forever
data.text: Even if you delete a log entry from the primary store, backups, replicas, and third-party log shippers may retain it for months. Assume anything written to a log is recoverable indefinitely.

items.question: Is logging request IDs safe?
items.answer: Yes. Request IDs are not sensitive and are essential for correlating logs across services. Log them at the start of every request.

items.question: What about logging exceptions?
items.answer: Exception messages can contain sensitive data. Use a custom exception handler that redacts sensitive fields from exception messages before logging.

items.question: Should I log user agent and IP address?
items.answer: User agent strings are generally safe. IP addresses may be considered PII under GDPR, so check your legal requirements. Consider hashing or truncating IPs if required.

items.question: How do I audit existing logs for sensitive data?
items.answer: Use a log scanning tool or regular expression to search for patterns like credit card numbers, social security numbers, and password fields. Run it on production log archives.

data.title: Implement a redaction policy
data.description: Add request logging to an ASP.NET Core API, but ensure sensitive fields are never written to logs.
steps: Identify all fields in your API requests that contain sensitive data
Create a redaction filter or middleware that masks these fields
Log only metadata: method, path, user ID, status, and duration
Write a unit test that sends a request with a password and asserts it does not appear in the log output
Scan existing production logs for leaked data and document findings
data.expectedOutcome: Logs contain enough information to debug issues without exposing secrets. The unit test guarantees the redaction policy is enforced.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Logs are a data store with the same security requirements as your database
Never log passwords, tokens, payment details, or raw request bodies
Use metadata-only logging for production; reserve detailed logging for controlled debug environments
Audit existing logs for sensitive data as part of your security review
data.takeaway: If you would not put it in the database, do not put it in the logs.
